analysis.one_liner: Hands federal coal-mining and reclamation enforcement entirely to state governments.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 23 cosponsors, advanced through a House subcommittee by a 6-2 vote in July 1996 but never got a vote in the full committee, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the 1977 law that governs strip mining for coal. In any state with a federally approved program, state rules would replace the federal law entirely: federal inspectors would stop overseeing mines, state regulators would be the only enforcers, and reviews would happen only in state courts. A mine that followed its permit would automatically count as meeting every environmental standard, enforcement actions would have to start within three years of a violation, and public roads built through mining areas would be exempt from the law altogether.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies. They would face only their own state regulators, with no federal inspections, no federal override of weak state enforcement, state-court-only review of state decisions, a three-year deadline that erases older enforcement cases, and a guarantee that a compliant permit shields them from any stricter environmental standard. Public road construction through mined areas would also escape federal reclamation rules.

how_it_helps.text: In states with approved programs, the state program would apply 'in lieu of' the federal mining act, and new federal rules would not take effect until the state amended its program and miners were given time to conform.

The bill would strip the federal Office of Surface Mining of oversight functions and give state regulatory authorities 'sole enforcement responsibility,' reviewable only under state administrative and judicial procedures.
An operation in compliance with its permit would be deemed in compliance with all environmental protection standards of the federal act and of state or federal programs, locking in the permit terms.
Any enforcement proceeding for a violation, fine, or penalty would be barred unless begun within three years of when the violation first occurred, wiping out older enforcement actions.
Public roads would be excluded from the act's definition of mining-related activities and areas, removing them from federal mining regulation.

The bill would repeal the provision preserving citizens' ability to sue to compel compliance with federal mining law, and would channel review of federal enforcement decisions into the district court containing the state's capital.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near coal mines and taxpayers generally. With no federal backstop, weakened state enforcement would mean more water pollution, poorer reclamation of mined land, and fewer avenues for citizens to force cleanup; taxpayers and neighboring landowners would inherit the costs of abandoned or poorly reclaimed mine sites.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near coal mines and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: State regulators would be the sole enforcers with review only under state law, removing the federal check that the 1977 law created after decades of unreclaimed strip mining damage.
The three-year statute of limitations would bar enforcement of older violations, allowing long-running problems to escape penalties.
Deeming permitted operations automatically compliant with all environmental standards would prevent regulators from applying tougher rules to mines already operating under older permits.
Removing public roads from the act's reach would exempt road construction in mining areas from the federal reclamation standards that otherwise apply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is mostly procedural for miners: one regulator instead of two and clear permit certainty. The cost is the loss of the federal enforcement backstop, citizens' suit rights, and the ability to correct older violations, all of which fall on the people who live around mines and on the land and water they depend on.

outcome.mechanism: The Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee approved an amended version by a 6-2 vote in July 1996, but the full House Resources Committee never took it up, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 21, 1995, and referred to the House Committee on Resources.
It was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which requested executive comment from the Interior Department and held hearings on November 9, 1995.
On July 18, 1996, the subcommittee held a markup and forwarded an amended bill to the full committee by a vote of 6 to 2.
The full Resources Committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the House floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1997, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People living near coal mines and the public kept the federal enforcement backstop, citizens' suit rights, and the ability to pursue older mining violations that this bill would have eliminated. Coal operators gained nothing because the bill never reached a floor vote.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Cubin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 original cosponsors.

for.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, marked up the bill, and forwarded an amended version to the full committee by a 6-2 vote on July 18, 1996.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Full committee chair and majority, 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a full-committee markup or floor action after the subcommittee forwarded the amended bill in July 1996, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship ran 20 Republicans to 3 Democrats, with the three Democrats coming from coal-producing districts; the subcommittee that advanced it voted 6-2.

industries.note: The bill would have made state regulators their sole enforcers, eliminated federal inspections, deemed permits fully compliant with environmental standards, barred enforcement after three years, and exempted public roads — benefits that come at the expense of enforcement for people living near mines.
The bill would have locked in state agencies as the exclusive, federally unreviewable channel for coal mine permitting and enforcement, replacing the current shared federal-state system.
